inds.name: Electronics and displays
mem: Samsung Electronics (Device eXperience), Samsung Display, Harman

scen.name: Armed stalemate (includes part of the succession with the regime intact)
All-out war on the Korean Peninsula
Leadership succession with the regime intact
A favorable end to the war
End of the war and full reopening
Regime collapse or civil war in Iran
A sustained standoff below the threshold of war
A deadly incident, then a patch-up

F2.w: A narrower "Korea discount" slightly improves funding conditions

F3.w: The Nuclear dominoes scenario is weighted about 40 percent to South Korea leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (arms-transfer ban, cut-off of nuclear fuel, credit-rating downgrade, tariff and export-control pressure) and the rest to cases in which only a decision is made or only Japan moves (almost no effect)

F4a.w: The Pyeongtaek, Icheon and Hwaseong plants are within range of North Korean multiple rocket launchers (such as the KN-09) and ballistic missiles. South Korean incomes −35%

F4d.w: Part of the cost of unification

T2.w: Inspections and higher insurance premiums; small effect on demand

T3.w: First year: the halt in HBM exports to Taiwan is offset by higher memory prices as Taiwanese DRAM production stops. Next two years: a small gain as HBM supply resumes and customers diversify away from Taiwan

T4.w: First year: loss of Chinese customers and plants in China plus a global recession (−35%). Next two years: with Taiwanese capacity lost, South Korean memory and foundries become alternative suppliers and recover part of the loss. The Chinese market does not recover

T5.w: Stable U.S.-China relations; export controls may ease

I4.w: Global slowdown. Disrupted supply of helium from Qatar

F3.w: Sanctions risk (smaller than for chips, since much of production is overseas)

F4a.w: Domestic plants and the home market paralyzed; South Korean incomes −35%

T3.w: Recovery after chip supply stops in the first year (−10%)

T4.w: Cut-off from Taiwanese chips and from assembly and sales in China lasts all three years

I4.w: Higher energy costs and weaker demand

P4.w: Poland is a major production base for South Korean appliances (Samsung in Wronki; LG Electronics in Mława and Wrocław)

P5.w: European demand collapses; appliance plants in Poland and Hungary

F3.w: Risk to tax credits and Energy Department loans for U.S. joint-venture plants

F4a.w: Disruption at domestic plants. U.S. and European plants keep running

T3.w: Recovery after first-year disruption from logistics and partial sanctions

T4.w: Chinese graphite and precursors stay cut off, but the gain from Chinese competitors leaving the U.S. market grows

I2.w: Lower oil prices weaken the incentive to buy electric vehicles

P4.w: A Baltic incident alone leaves EU carbon rules intact, and energy-storage demand served by the Wrocław, Poland, plant (about 80 GWh, Europe's largest EV battery plant) partly offsets the impact. The plant is far from the Baltic

P5.w: European plants lie close to the war zone and European demand collapses

F3.w: Tariff pressure from the United States, the largest market

F4a.w: Disruption at the Ulsan and Gwangju plants and in the parts network, and a collapse of the home market. Overseas plants keep running

F4d.w: Part of the North Korean market

T3.w: Recovery after a first-year chip shortage (pricing protects margins, as in 2021)

T4.w: Chip cut-off and global recession last two to three years

U3.w: Hyundai did not exercise its right to buy back the St. Petersburg plant in January 2026, so any return to Russia starts from scratch (Chinese brands dominate the market)

U4.w: Weaker European demand (a sizable share of Hyundai and Kia sales)

I2.w: Lower fuel prices and recovering Middle East sales (about 5 percent of Hyundai and Kia sales)

I4.w: Shock to South Korean incomes (−5% versus the status quo) and loss of Middle East markets

P5.w: Disruption to European sales (about 15 percent; ACEA, January–May 2026) and to the Czech and Slovak plants

F3.w: If South Korea withdraws from the NPT, cooperation on U.S. Navy ship maintenance (MASGA) shrinks

F4a.w: Revenue from about three years of order backlog is recognized as work progresses, so it does not collapse, but war-risk insurance, labor mobilization and delayed orders squeeze profits

T2.w: Western shipowners gradually shun Chinese shipyards

T3.w: Little change in the first year because of order backlogs; over the next two years, orders diverted from Chinese shipyards show up in revenue

T4.w: Orders shift from sanctioned Chinese shipyards to South Korea, but first-year costs are heavy: the shock to the South Korean economy, insurance and steel. Wide range for this cell

U4.w: Higher European demand for LNG brings orders for LNG carriers

I2.w: Demand for tankers and LNG carriers normalizes (with order backlogs, only part shows up in 2030 revenue)

P5.w: Order backlogs sustain revenue, but fixed-price contracts are hit by steel and labor cost shocks (as in 2022)

F5.w: A U.S.–North Korea deal that leaves South Korea out raises demand for self-reliant defense

F2.w: Defense is export-driven, so easing tensions at home has little effect

F3.w: If South Korea withdraws from the NPT, a U.S. ban on arms transfers disrupts exports that contain U.S. parts or licenses (such as GE engines in the KF-21 and FA-50). Partly offset by higher defense spending

F4a.w: Southern plants such as Changwon and Gumi run at full capacity for domestic wartime procurement. Partly offset by penalties for late export deliveries to Poland and others. Wide range for this cell

F4b.w: Possible defense budget increase after a localized clash (budget growth was raised for 2011 after the 2010 Cheonan sinking)

T3.w: Bound by contracts in the first year, then export growth from Asian rearmament over the next two years

T4.w: A shock to the South Korean economy in the first year, then a surge in global defense demand (as with South Korean defense exports after 2022)

T5.w: Defense demand falls slightly as tensions ease

U2.w: Even after a ceasefire with Western troops deployed, European rearmament (NATO's 3.5 percent defense spending target) continues

U6.w: The risk of a new invasion remains, so European rearmament continues

U3.w: Peace on Russia's terms speeds rearmament by its neighbors, but preference for European suppliers (SAFE loans) limits South Korea's share

U4.w: Emergency European procurement. Within three years, output is capped by K2 and K9 production lines, and new orders turn into revenue two to four years later

U5.w: Orders signed in 2022–2025 are delivered through about 2030, and Poland spends about 4.7 percent of GDP on defense. Only new orders slow

I2.w: The Cheongung-II (KM-SAM) Gulf contracts (10 batteries for the UAE, 10 for Saudi Arabia, 8 for Iraq) are already signed and, capped by production capacity of about eight batteries a year, will be delivered through about 2029. Postwar restocking continues

I4.w: Emergency purchases of air-defense weapons by Gulf states under attack

P2.w: After the September 2025 drone incursion, Poland's counter-drone program (about 15 billion zlotys) went to Polish and European firms (PGZ, Kongsberg). Incident-response budgets flow to European suppliers first (SAFE), leaving a small share for South Korea

P3.w: A 30-day crisis that ends without fighting. Preference for European suppliers limits South Korea's share

P4.w: Emergency European procurement (K2, K9, Chunmoo) after an attack on NATO territory

P5.w: Wartime demand surges (in 2022, deliveries began four months after signing by diverting equipment allocated to the South Korean military). Partly offset by delivery risk at Polish ports and a global recession

P6.w: New orders slow as tensions ease (contracted orders are still delivered)

F3.w: Higher electricity prices if nuclear fuel supplies are restricted (energy-intensive industries)

F4a.w: Damage to the Ulsan, Yeosu and Daesan complexes and a collapse of the home market. Partly offset by soaring prices for petroleum products

T3.w: Recovery after weaker Chinese demand in the first year

T4.w: China, the largest export market, remains cut off

U3.w: If sanctions ease and Russian petroleum products return to Europe, diesel margins fall. Partly offset by lower petrochemical feedstock costs as Russian naphtha returns

U4.w: A risk premium lifts diesel margins

I2.w: The current gain in refining margins (2026 consensus operating profit for S-Oil about 5 trillion won, versus 288 billion won in 2025) disappears. Even if the war continued, though, restored capacity would erase much of the gain by 2030 (brokerage forecasts: $30 a barrel in the second half of 2026 → $19 in 2027)

I6.w: The strait reopens, but seizures and transit controls continue, so only part of the margin gain disappears

I3.w: The strait remains a risk zone, so this is close to the status quo

I4.w: When Gulf exports fell to about 36 percent of prewar levels in March–May 2026, South Korean refiners switched to U.S. and Mediterranean crude and posted record margins (S-Oil's complex refining margin above $41 a barrel). A government cap on oil prices limited part of the gain

P5.w: Refining margins spike as in 2022 (record profits for South Korean refiners). Same principle as U.S. refining

F4a.w: Airspace closures halt air travel and domestic port volumes collapse. Ships operating abroad and higher freight rates partly offset the loss

F4d.w: Routes and logistics to North Korea

T2.w: Detours around the Taiwan Strait raise freight rates slightly

T3.w: Normalization after a first-year rise in freight rates (+33%)

T4.w: Freight and passenger volumes collapse in the first year; afterward, soaring freight rates let shipping recover part of the loss

U2.w: South Korean airlines avoid Russian airspace on their own, adding about two hours and 45 minutes to European routes. A guaranteed ceasefire could let them fly over it again

U6.w: Half the effect of a guaranteed ceasefire

U3.w: Flights over Russia resume. If European airlines regain the airspace too, competition on Korea–Europe routes intensifies again and the advantage shrinks

I2.w: Fuel savings are offset as wartime air-cargo and tanker rates normalize

I4.w: Jet fuel spikes and Middle East airspace and hubs close. Partly offset by higher shipping rates

P5.w: European routes and freight volumes collapse; fuel costs spike

F2.w: Bank profits showed no clear change even during the 2018 thaw. A narrower "Korea discount" shows up mainly in share prices

F3.w: Sanctions risk, capital flight and a credit-rating downgrade

F4a.w: Massive bad loans as South Korean incomes fall 35%

F4d.w: Cost of unification and of absorbing North Korea's financial system

T3.w: Recovery after higher loan losses in the first year

T4.w: Bad loans from the South Korean income shock last two to three years

U4.w: Risk aversion, a weaker won and higher loan losses (South Korean incomes −0.8%)

I2.w: South Korean incomes recover (+3.5% versus the status quo)

I4.w: Shock to South Korean incomes (−5% versus the status quo)

F4a.w: About 70 percent of the world's DRAM and about 80 percent of its HBM are made in South Korea (TrendForce, Counterpoint 2025). Nvidia and AMD GPU production stalls for lack of HBM (Micron gains)

T3.w: Recovery after TSMC wafer supply stops in the first year (−46%)

T4.w: Prolonged loss of TSMC capacity and a cut-off from the Chinese market. Samsung and Intel foundries partly fill the gap

T5.w: Chinese sales recover as export controls ease

F4a.w: Disrupted supply of OLED panels and memory to Apple and others (Samsung Display, LG Display)

T3.w: Recovery after first-year disruption to iPhone chip supply

T4.w: TSMC supply and Chinese assembly and sales remain cut off

F4a.w: Asian LNG prices fall as demand collapses in South Korea, the world's third-largest LNG importer

T3.w: Recovery after weaker demand in the first year

U6.w: An unguaranteed ceasefire leaves most sanctions in place, so the effect is half that of a guaranteed ceasefire

U3.w: The EU legislated a ban on Russian gas imports in January 2026 (to be completed by the end of 2027), so demand for U.S. LNG holds even after the war ends. Russian crude is bound by OPEC+ quotas, so only its discount narrows

U4.w: Higher oil and gas prices; more European demand for U.S. LNG

I2.w: Compared at 2030 levels: Brent at about $75–85 if the war continues (the EIA projects a fall to $74 by the fourth quarter of 2027), about $65 if it ends

I6.w: About half the effect of a full reopening

I3.w: The strait remains a risk zone, so oil prices are slightly higher

I4.w: Oil prices spike as Gulf exports halve (above $120 possible in the first year)

P4.w: Higher European gas prices; more demand for U.S. LNG

P5.w: Oil and gas prices spike in a European energy crisis

F4a.w: South Korea's petroleum product exports (about 1.34 million barrels a day in 2024) stop, lifting Asian product margins

T3.w: A small margin gain in the first year, then normalization

T4.w: Higher margins from the loss of Asian refining capacity are offset by lower demand

U3.w: If Russian diesel returns to Europe, U.S. refiners' diesel export margins to Europe fall

I2.w: The gain in product margins disappears, though it would shrink substantially by 2030 even if the war continued

P4.w: Risk that Russian diesel exports from the port of Primorsk are blocked if the Baltic region is seized

P5.w: Disrupted European refining and a spike in diesel margins

F3.w: South Korea is a major Foreign Military Sales customer (F-35A, Apache and others). NPT withdrawal would bring an arms-transfer ban

F4a.w: Capped by production capacity in the first year, then a surge in demand to replenish munitions and equipment

T3.w: A small effect in the first year because of existing contracts; over the next two years, higher defense budgets and arms sales to Asia show up in revenue. Partly offset by lower Boeing sales to China

T4.w: A small decline in the first year, capped by production capacity (−5%); over the next two years revenue surges with expanded wartime production (as for European and South Korean defense firms after 2022). Partly offset by weaker demand for commercial aircraft

U2.w: End of NATO purchases of U.S. weapons for Ukraine (PURL, more than $4 billion pledged in 2025)

U3.w: European purchases of U.S. weapons continue

U4.w: Emergency demand for munitions and air-defense weapons (capped by production capacity in the first year)

U5.w: End of demand for support to Ukraine

I2.w: Lower consumption of interceptor missiles and other munitions

P4.w: Emergency European purchases of U.S. weapons and munitions (capped by production capacity in the first year)

F4a.w: GM's South Korean plants (small SUVs for the U.S. market) shut down; South Korean parts supply disrupted. Partly offset by share gains as Hyundai and Kia exports to the U.S. stop

T3.w: Recovery after a first-year chip shortage

T4.w: Chip cut-off and recession last two to three years

I4.w: Gasoline prices spike and the economy slows

P5.w: U.S. incomes −8%; losses in European business

F4a.w: Korea routes suspended (Delta–Korean Air joint venture)

T3.w: Recovery after first-year cuts to trans-Pacific routes

T4.w: Partial recovery after a sharp first-year fall

I2.w: Lower jet fuel prices. But airlines pass much of any fuel cost increase on to fares (Delta recovered about 60 percent of its second-quarter fuel cost increase and expects an operating margin of 11–13 percent even during the war)

I6.w: About half the effect of a full reopening

I4.w: Even in the real shock of spring 2026, Delta's full-year profit outlook was above its 2025 level

P5.w: Collapse of transatlantic routes and a spike in fuel costs

T4.w: Loan losses from the U.S. income shock last two to three years

F4a.w: South Korea is a major importer of U.S. corn, wheat and beef

T3.w: China shifts soybean purchases to Brazil, so recovery is slow, as in 2018

T5.w: Chinese commitments to buy farm goods, as in the 2020 Phase One trade deal

U2.w: Grain prices fall as Ukrainian grain exports return to normal

U3.w: Fertilizer prices fall as grain exports and Russian fertilizer supplies (potash, ammonia) return to normal

U4.w: Risk to Black Sea grain exports raises grain prices

U5.w: Ukrainian grain exports return to normal

I2.w: Industry basket: Deere, ADM, Bunge, Corteva, CF and Mosaic. As Gulf urea (about 43 percent of world seaborne trade) and ammonia supplies normalize, fertilizer makers' profits (CF, Mosaic) fall, partly offset as lower costs help farm machinery and grain trading

P5.w: Disrupted European production raises grain and fertilizer prices
